Theo van Doesburg. A Dutch painter, architect, and theorist who lived from 1883 to 1931 and co-founded De Stijl, one of modernism's most radical movements. Through both his artwork and his editorial work on the De Stijl journal, van Doesburg became the movement's primary theorist and ambassador, defining its geometrical aesthetics and utopian vision. His influence extended across painting, graphic design, and architecture, making him a pivotal figure in early twentieth-century modernism.

Born Christiaan Emil Marie Küpper in 1883, he adopted the pseudonym Theo van Doesburg for his artistic career. Van Doesburg founded De Stijl in 1917 with Piet Mondrian and others, establishing the journal as the movement's intellectual center. He developed De Stijl's core aesthetic principles: reduction to primary colors—red, blue, yellow—plus black, white, and gray; geometric abstraction; and the elimination of perspective.

He served as editor of the De Stijl journal from its inception, commissioning and promoting the works of artists, architects, and designers aligned with the movement's vision. In the mid-nineteen-twenties, van Doesburg created an Elementarism variation of De Stijl, introducing diagonal lines to challenge the purely horizontal-vertical orthogonal aesthetic. He designed graphics, paintings, and architectural concepts that unified art and practical design, embodying the modernist belief that geometric abstraction could transform society.

Van Doesburg collaborated with the Bauhaus and other avant-garde institutions, spreading De Stijl's influence across Europe during the nineteen-twenties. He died unexpectedly at age 47, just as De Stijl was fragmenting, but left an intellectual legacy that shaped abstract art, graphic design, and architecture for decades. His writings and manifestos were as influential as his art; he articulated the philosophical basis for geometric abstraction and the belief that radical formal reduction could serve human liberation.
